lessons.title: Big-O notation
lessons.explain: Big-O describes how runtime or extra memory grows as input size n grows. Analyze the structure of the algorithm rather than memorizing labels: identify loops/recursion, account for nested work, and state meaningful best/average/worst cases when they differ.
lessons.example:
nums = [4, 1, 7, 3]
# O(n): one pass
steps = 0
for x in nums:
    steps += 1
print(steps)

# O(n^2): nested passes
pairs = 0
for i in nums:
    for j in nums:
        pairs += 1
print(pairs)
objectives: Describe how an algorithm's runtime or memory grows with input size
Understand and apply Algorithm analysis & Big-O in Python.
Explain how time complexity changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect time complexity with space complexity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Confusing the WORST-case complexity with typical or best-case performance -- Big-O usually describes the worst case.
examples:

# O(n): one pass

for x in nums:
    steps += 1
print(steps)

# O(n^2): nested passes
pairs = 0
for i in nums:
    for j in nums:
        pairs += 1
print(pairs)

nums = [10,20,30]
print(nums[0])

nums = [3,1,9,2]
best = nums[0]

n = 64

    steps += 1

nums = [1,2,1,3,2]

print(len(seen))

lessons.title: Arrays
objectives: Explain array storage and access time complexity
Understand and apply Arrays / Python lists in Python.
Explain how array changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect array with index and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Python lists act as dynamic arrays for most interview problems. Index access is O(1); traversal is O(n); inserting or deleting in the middle can shift later elements and cost O(n).
examples:
arr = [10, 20, 30]
print(arr[1])     # 20 -- O(1) access
arr.insert(1, 99)  # O(n) -- shifts 20 and 30 over

nums = [1,3,4]
nums.insert(1,2)
nums.pop()
print(nums)

nums = [1,2,3,4]
left, right = 0, len(nums)-1
while left < right:
    nums[left], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[left]
    left += 1; right -= 1
print(nums)

nums=[2,4,6,8]
prefix=[0]
for x in nums: prefix.append(prefix[-1]+x)
print(prefix)
commonMistakes: Assuming inserting into the middle of an array is as cheap as accessing an element -- access is O(1), but insertion/deletion in the middle is O(n).
lessons.careerRelevance: Arrays are the most fundamental data structure, underlying many others.

lessons.title: Linked lists
objectives: Explain how linked lists differ from arrays

Explain how linked list changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: A linked list stores elements as nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node -- not contiguous in memory. Inserting or deleting at the front is O(1), unlike an array's O(n) shift.
examples:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

# 1 -> 2 -> 3
head = Node(1)
head.next = Node(2)
head.next.next = Node(3)

class Node:
    def __init__(self,value,next_node=None): self.value,self.next=value,next_node
head=Node(1,Node(2,Node(3)))
print(head.next.value)

class Node:
    def __init__(self,value,next_node=None): self.value,self.next=value,next_node
head=Node(1,Node(2,Node(3)))
cur=head
while cur:
    print(cur.value)
    cur=cur.next

class Node:
    def __init__(self,value,next_node=None): self.value,self.next=value,next_node
head=Node(2,Node(3))
head=Node(1,head)
print(head.value, head.next.value)

class Node:
    def __init__(self,value,next_node=None): self.value,self.next=value,next_node
head=Node(1,Node(2,Node(3)))
prev=None
while head:
    nxt=head.next; head.next=prev; prev=head; head=nxt
print(prev.value, prev.next.value, prev.next.next.value)

class Node:
    def __init__(self,value,next_node=None): self.value,self.next=value,next_node
head=Node(1,Node(2,Node(3,Node(4,Node(5)))))
slow=fast=head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow=slow.next; fast=fast.next.next
print(slow.value)
commonMistakes: Assuming linked lists support O(1) random access like arrays do -- they don't; reaching the nth node takes O(n) time.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding linked lists' trade-offs vs arrays is a classic, frequently-tested interview topic.

lessons.title: Stacks & queues
objectives: Explain LIFO and FIFO ordering and when each is useful
Understand and apply Stacks & queues in Python.
Explain how stack changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect stack with queue and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A stack is Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) -- the most recently added item is removed first, like a stack of plates. A queue is First-In-First-Out (FIFO) -- the first item added is the first removed, like a line of people.
examples:
# stack: push/pop from the same end
stack = []
stack.append(1); stack.append(2)
stack.pop()   # removes 2 (LIFO)

# queue: add at one end, remove from the other
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append(1); q.append(2)
q.popleft()   # removes 1 (FIFO)

stack=[]
stack.append("A"); stack.append("B")
print(stack.pop())

from collections import deque
q=deque(['A','B']); q.append('C')
print(q.popleft(), list(q))

from collections import deque
d=deque([2,3]); d.appendleft(1); d.append(4)
print(list(d))
commonMistakes: Using a plain list's .pop(0) to simulate a queue -- this is O(n), not O(1); use collections.deque for real O(1) queue operations.
lessons.careerRelevance: Stacks and queues underlie countless real systems: undo history, browser back-buttons, task scheduling, and more.

lessons.explanation: A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes, each with one parent (except the root) and any number of children. A binary tree limits each node to at most two children.
examples:
class Node:
    def __init__(self,value,left=None,right=None): self.value,self.left,self.right=value,left,right
root=Node(2,Node(1),Node(3))
print(root.left.value, root.right.value)

root=Node(2,Node(1),Node(3))
def inorder(node): return inorder(node.left)+[node.value]+inorder(node.right) if node else []
print(inorder(root))

lessons.title: Graphs
objectives: Represent graphs and understand basic traversal
Understand and apply Graphs with BFS & DFS in Python.
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Dijkstra shortest path, minimum spanning tree (Prim/Kruskal), union-find / disjoint set.
lessons.explanation: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges -- more general than a tree, since cycles and multiple paths are allowed. Graphs can be directed (edges have a direction) or undirected.
examples:
# adjacency list representation:
graph = {
    'A': ['B', 'C'],
    'B': ['A', 'D'],
    'C': ['A'],
    'D': ['B']
}

g={'A':['B','C'],'B':['D'],'C':['D'],'D':[]}
stack=['A']; seen=set(); order=[]
while stack:
    node=stack.pop()
    if node in seen: continue
    seen.add(node); order.append(node); stack.extend(reversed(g[node]))
print(order)

g={1:[2],2:[3],3:[]}
target=3; stack=[1]; seen=set(); found=False
while stack:
    node=stack.pop()
    if node==target: found=True; break
    if node in seen: continue
    seen.add(node); stack.extend(g[node])
print(found)
commonMistakes: Not tracking visited nodes during traversal -- this causes infinite loops on graphs with cycles, unlike trees which have none.
lessons.careerRelevance: Graphs model networks, dependencies, maps, and social connections -- extremely common in real systems. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Searching algorithms
objectives: Compare linear and binary search
Understand and apply Searching: linear & binary in Python.
Explain how linear search changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect linear search with binary search and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Linear search checks each element one at a time -- O(n), works on any list. Binary search repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the middle element -- O(log n), but REQUIRES the data to already be sorted.
examples:
def binary_search(sorted_arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(sorted_arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if sorted_arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif sorted_arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

def binary_search(nums,target):
    low,high=0,len(nums)-1
    while low<=high:
        mid=(low+high)//2
        if nums[mid]==target: return mid
        if nums[mid]<target: low=mid+1
        else: high=mid-1
    return -1
print(binary_search([1,3,5,7,9],7))

def first_at_least(nums,target):
    low,high=0,len(nums)
    while low<high:
        mid=(low+high)//2
        if nums[mid]>=target: high=mid
        else: low=mid+1
    return low
print(first_at_least([1,3,5,7],4))

from bisect import bisect_left
nums=[1,3,5,7]
print(bisect_left(nums,5), bisect_left(nums,4))

nums=[1,3,5,7,9,11,13]; target=11
low,high=0,len(nums)-1
while low<=high:
    mid=(low+high)//2
    print(low,mid,high,nums[mid])
    if nums[mid]==target: break
    if nums[mid]<target: low=mid+1
    else: high=mid-1
commonMistakes: Applying binary search to unsorted data -- it silently gives wrong results, since the halving logic assumes sorted order.
lessons.careerRelevance: Binary search is one of the most fundamental, frequently-tested algorithms in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Sorting II — Merge sort & quicksort
lessons.explanation: Merge sort divides the input, recursively sorts each half, then merges sorted halves. Quicksort chooses a pivot and partitions values around it.
objectives: Understand and apply Merge sort & quicksort in Python.
Explain how merge sort changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect merge sort with quicksort and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
def merge_sort(nums):
    if len(nums)<=1: return nums[:]
    mid=len(nums)//2; left=merge_sort(nums[:mid]); right=merge_sort(nums[mid:])
    out=[]; i=j=0
    while i<len(left) and j<len(right):
        if left[i]<=right[j]: out.append(left[i]); i+=1
        else: out.append(right[j]); j+=1
    return out+left[i:]+right[j:]
print(merge_sort([5,1,4,2]))

def quick_sort(nums):
    if len(nums)<=1: return nums[:]
    pivot=nums[len(nums)//2]
    left=[x for x in nums if x<pivot]
    middle=[x for x in nums if x==pivot]
    right=[x for x in nums if x>pivot]
    return quick_sort(left)+middle+quick_sort(right)
print(quick_sort([5,1,4,2,4]))

a=[1,4,7]; b=[2,3,8]; i=j=0; out=[]
while i<len(a) and j<len(b):
    if a[i]<=b[j]: out.append(a[i]); i+=1
    else: out.append(b[j]); j+=1
out += a[i:]+b[j:]
print(out)

nums=[7,2,5,3,5]; pivot=5
print([x for x in nums if x<pivot])
print([x for x in nums if x==pivot])
print([x for x in nums if x>pivot])

nums=[9,1,7,3,8,2]
print(sorted(nums))
commonMistakes: Saying quicksort is always O(n log n).
lessons.explain: Merge sort divides the input, recursively sorts each half, then merges sorted halves. Quicksort chooses a pivot and partitions values around it.

lessons.title: Recursion & backtracking
objectives: Use recursion safely and apply choose-explore-unchoose backtracking to search problems
Explain how base case changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect base case with recursive state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to smaller versions of itself. A correct recursive solution needs a base case and progress toward that base case.
lessons.example:
def subsets(nums):
    out = []
    path = []
    def dfs(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(path.copy())
            return
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.append(nums[i])
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return out

print(subsets([1, 2]))
commonMistakes: Forgetting to undo mutable state after exploring a branch, or writing recursion that does not move toward a base case.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

description: The core of coding interviews — patterns that solve whole problem classes.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you approach a DSA problem you've never seen before in an interview?
interviewPreparation.a: Restate the problem in your own words to confirm understanding, work through a small concrete example by hand, identify a brute-force approach first even if inefficient, then look for patterns (sorted data suggests two pointers or binary search; 'have I seen this before' suggests a hash set) to optimize from there -- rather than guessing at a clever solution immediately.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose a hash map over a balanced tree for lookups?
interviewPreparation.a: A hash map gives O(1) average-case lookup/insert/delete, versus a tree's O(log n) -- so for pure lookup speed with no ordering requirement, a hash map usually wins. Choose a tree instead when you need ordered traversal, range queries, or predictable worst-case performance, since a hash map's worst case can degrade under pathological input.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you explain time complexity to someone non-technical?
interviewPreparation.a: It describes how the AMOUNT OF WORK grows as the input gets bigger, not the exact speed on one machine. An analogy: searching a phone book by flipping through every page (linear) versus jumping to the right section alphabetically (much faster growth) -- as the phone book gets 10x bigger, one approach's work barely changes while the other's grows a lot.

interviewPreparation.q: What's your process for debugging a solution that fails on some test cases but not others?
interviewPreparation.a: Look specifically at what's different about the failing cases -- empty input, a single element, duplicates, or boundary values are common culprits. Trace through the failing case by hand with the actual algorithm logic, rather than guessing, since the specific pattern of which cases fail usually points directly at the bug.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does knowing multiple approaches to the same problem matter, beyond just solving it once?
interviewPreparation.a: Different approaches have different trade-offs (time vs space, average vs worst case, simplicity vs performance), and real systems have different constraints. Being able to discuss why you'd choose one over another demonstrates genuine understanding of the trade-offs, not just memorization of one solution.

careerApplications: The core of coding interview rounds (OAs and live coding).

capstone.title: Benchmark and compare 3 approaches to the same problem
capstone.description: Pick a classic problem (e.g. finding duplicates, computing the k most frequent elements, or detecting a cycle in a graph). Implement it three different ways with genuinely different time/space trade-offs (e.g. a brute-force O(n^2) approach, a hash-based O(n) approach, and a sorting-based O(n log n) approach). Measure and compare their actual runtime on inputs of increasing size, and write up which approach you'd actually choose in a real system and why.
deliverables: Three distinct, correctly-working implementations of the same problem with different complexity classes
A benchmark script measuring actual runtime across at least 3 input sizes (e.g. 100, 10,000, 1,000,000 elements)
A short written comparison explaining WHY the runtimes diverge as input size grows, tied to each approach's real complexity
A clear recommendation: which approach you'd actually use in production, and under what conditions you'd choose differently (e.g. very small n, memory-constrained environment)
capstone.portfolioTips: This project demonstrates something a simple 'I solved LeetCode problem X' claim doesn't: that you understand WHY complexity matters in practice, not just how to state Big-O notation -- explicitly call this out in your README.
